```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1105)

# The Capital One card portfolio used all morning (simulated).
n <- 500
fico <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 690, 50), 560), 830))
util <- round(pmin(pmax(160 - 0.15 * fico + rnorm(n, 0, 12), 0), 100), 1)
cards <- tibble(fico, util)
reg <- lm(util ~ fico, data = cards)
```

## This morning

**Hour 1 · Theory**

- The linear regression model: a line, plus what the line misses
- Ordinary Least Squares (OLS): which line, and why that one
- Sums of squares: splitting the variation in $Y$ into *explained* and *missed*
- $R^2$ and the standard error of the regression

**Hour 2 · Code**

- Building OLS by hand in R, then checking it against `lm()`
- Rebuilding $R^2$ from sums of squares
- Watching the slope bounce from sample to sample: what "Std. Error" means

**Reading:** Stock & Watson §4.1–4.3, §4.5 · **Assigned today:** Classwork 3-1

::: {.notes}
Frame the day in one sentence: for six weeks we have described one variable
at a time; today we describe how one variable moves with another, and we do
it with a single line.

Tell her the destination up front. By Tuesday she should be able to read every

## Where we are

Two weeks ago, in Classwork 2-1, you computed a **correlation** between bank
branches and denials.

. . .

Correlation answered: *do they move together, and how tightly?*

It could not answer: **by how much?**

. . .

> If a borrower's credit score were 50 points lower, how much more of their
> credit line would we expect them to be using?

That is a question about a **slope**. Regression is the tool that estimates
slopes.

::: {.notes}
Connect to what she already owns. She computed cov(X,Y) and rho by hand. The
OLS slope is cov over var, and she will see that formula in fifteen minutes.
Promise it now: "you already know 80% of the formula."

Correlation is unit-free on purpose. A slope is in units: percentage points
of utilization per FICO point. That is exactly what makes it useful to a
business.
:::

## The job: Capital One, Card Credit Risk

You are an analyst on a **credit card credit risk team**. Your manager asks:

> "How does credit utilization move with FICO score in our portfolio?"

. . .

| Variable | Meaning | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `util` | **Utilization**: balance ÷ credit line | percent (0–100) |
| `fico` | FICO credit score at the last refresh | points (300–850) |

. . .

High utilization is an early-warning sign: borrowers who max out their lines
miss payments more often. If utilization tracks FICO, the team can watch
lower-score accounts more closely and size credit-line increases more
carefully.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
The data are **simulated**: 500 made-up accounts. The setting is real; the
numbers are not.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes on why this question would actually be asked. Credit risk teams
decide credit-line increases and decreases, watch-lists, and collections
strategy. Utilization is one of the strongest predictors of default in card
portfolios. So the question is realistic.

Plant a seed for later: FICO is partly computed FROM utilization. So this
regression describes an association; it does not say which causes which.
Come back to it if she asks; otherwise it lives in the "what can go wrong"
discussion on Tuesday.
:::

## Look before you fit

```{r}
#| label: scatter
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(cards, aes(fico, util)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, colour = "#2C3E50") +
  labs(
    x = "FICO score",
    y = "Utilization (%)",
    title = "500 card accounts (simulated)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
```

Downward and noisy. A line will summarize the *trend*; it will not pass
through the points.

::: {.notes}
Ask her before advancing: "If you had to draw one straight line through this
cloud with a ruler, where would it go?" Have her sketch it on the chalkboard.
That sketch is the thing OLS is about to formalize.

Point out the spread: two accounts at the same FICO can have very different
utilization. That vertical spread is the error term, and it never goes away.
:::

## The linear regression model

$$
\underbrace{Y_i}_{\text{outcome}} \;=\;
\underbrace{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i}_{\text{population regression line}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{u_i}_{\text{error term}}
$$

| Symbol | Name | In our problem |
|---|---|---|
| $Y_i$ | dependent variable, outcome | utilization of account $i$ |
| $X_i$ | independent variable, regressor | FICO score of account $i$ |
| $\beta_0$ | intercept | predicted $Y$ when $X = 0$ |
| $\beta_1$ | **slope** | change in $Y$ for a **one-unit** increase in $X$ |
| $u_i$ | error | everything else that moves utilization |

. . .

Greek letters with no hat are the **population truth**: fixed, unknown.
With a hat ($\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, \hat Y_i$), they are **estimates
from our sample**. R prints hats.

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §4.1. This is the most important slide of the day; slow down.

The error term u is not a "mistake." It is every other cause of utilization:
income shocks, spending habits, a car repair. We do not observe it.

Same population/sample distinction as Day 4: mu vs x-bar, sigma vs s. Now
beta vs beta-hat. She should hear the parallel out loud.

Write on the board: beta_1 = "rise over run" = (change in Y)/(change in X).
:::

## You Try 1 — Read a fitted line

Suppose the fitted line for our portfolio is

$$
\widehat{\text{util}} = 152.5 - 0.139 \times \text{fico}
$$

**(a)** Predict utilization for an account with FICO 650, and for one with
FICO 750.

**(b)** How much lower is predicted utilization for the 750 account? Where
does that number come from?

**(c)** In one sentence, what does $-0.139$ mean? Use units.

**(d)** The intercept says an account with FICO 0 uses 152.5% of its line.
Why should we not believe that?

::: {.notes}
Four minutes, by hand. Calculator allowed.

(b) is the point: 100 points times -0.139 is -13.9. The slope times the
change in X gives the change in the prediction. She should see that she
did not need part (a) to answer (b).

(d) Two answers, both right: FICO scores run 300-850, so 0 is not a real
score; and nobody in our data is anywhere near 0, so we are extrapolating
far outside the sample. Utilization over 100% is the giveaway.
:::

## Solution 1

**(a)** $152.5 - 0.139(650) = 152.5 - 90.35 = 62.15\%$ ·
$\;152.5 - 0.139(750) = 152.5 - 104.25 = 48.25\%$

**(b)** $62.15 - 48.25 = 13.9$ points lower, which is $100 \times 0.139$.
Slope × change in $X$ = change in the prediction.

**(c)** Each additional FICO point is associated with **0.139 percentage
points lower** utilization, on average. (Equivalently: 1.39 points lower per
10 FICO points.)

**(d)** FICO scores start at 300, and no account in the data is near 0. The
intercept anchors the height of the line; reading it literally is
**extrapolation**.

::: {.notes}
Insist on "associated with" and "on average" in (c). Not "causes," not
"every borrower." Those two phrases do a lot of honest work.

The intercept trap returns in the homework (the intercept is at DTI = 0,
which is at least possible). Flag that now.
:::

## Which line? Ordinary Least Squares

```{r}
#| label: resid-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(7)
few <- slice_sample(cards, n = 40)
few_reg <- lm(util ~ fico, data = few)
ggplot(few, aes(fico, util)) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(xend = fico, yend = fitted(few_reg)),
    colour = "#E74C3C",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = coef(few_reg)[1],
    slope = coef(few_reg)[2],
    colour = "#18BC9C",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = "#2C3E50") +
  labs(x = "FICO score", y = "Utilization (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
```

Each red segment is a **residual**: $\hat u_i = Y_i - \hat Y_i$, the actual
value minus the line's prediction. OLS chooses the line that makes

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat u_i^{\,2} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(Y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 X_i\right)^2
\quad \textbf{as small as possible.}
$$

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §4.2. Forty accounts, so the segments are visible.

Why square? Two reasons, both said plainly. (1) Positive and negative misses
would cancel if we just added them. (2) Squaring makes the minimization
solvable with a closed-form formula, which is next slide.

The residual u-hat is the sample version of the error u. Same hat rule.
:::

## The OLS formulas

The minimization has a closed-form answer:

$$
\hat\beta_1 \;=\; \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)(Y_i - \bar Y)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2}
\;=\; \frac{s_{XY}}{s_X^2}
\qquad\qquad
\hat\beta_0 \;=\; \bar Y - \hat\beta_1 \bar X
$$

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**The slope** is the sample covariance of $X$ and $Y$ divided by the sample
variance of $X$. You computed both in Classwork 2-1.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**The intercept** makes the line pass through the point of means
$(\bar X, \bar Y)$. Every OLS line does.
:::
:::

. . .

Shorthand we'll use all week:
$\;S_{xx} = \sum (X_i - \bar X)^2 \quad S_{xy} = \sum (X_i - \bar X)(Y_i - \bar Y)$,
so $\hat\beta_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$.

::: {.notes}
We do not derive this; it is calculus (Stock & Watson Appendix 4.2). Tell
her that it is derived, that the derivation is two partial derivatives set
to zero, and that she does not need it for this course.

The n-1 in s_XY and s_X^2 cancels top and bottom, which is why S_xy/S_xx
gives the same number. Show that on the board in one line.

"Passes through the means" is worth a picture: put a dot at (x-bar, y-bar)
on the scatter and draw the line through it.
:::

## You Try 2 — OLS by hand

Five accounts. $X$ = missed payments in the last 12 months; $Y$ = utilization (%).

| Account | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $X_i$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| $Y_i$ | 30 | 38 | 52 | 58 | 72 |

**(a)** Compute $\bar X$ and $\bar Y$.

**(b)** Make a table with columns $X_i - \bar X$, $\;Y_i - \bar Y$,
$\;(X_i - \bar X)^2$, $\;(X_i - \bar X)(Y_i - \bar Y)$. Sum the last two
columns to get $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$.

**(c)** Compute $\hat\beta_1$ and $\hat\beta_0$. Interpret $\hat\beta_1$.

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes. This is the core skill of the homework. Let her struggle with
the table layout; the table IS the method.

Answers on the next slide. Common error: forgetting to subtract the mean
before multiplying in the cross-product column.
:::

## Solution 2

**(a)** $\bar X = 10/5 = 2$ · $\bar Y = 250/5 = 50$

**(b)**

| $i$ | $X_i - \bar X$ | $Y_i - \bar Y$ | $(X_i - \bar X)^2$ | $(X_i - \bar X)(Y_i - \bar Y)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | −2 | −20 | 4 | 40 |
| 2 | −1 | −12 | 1 | 12 |
| 3 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 8 | 1 | 8 |
| 5 | 2 | 22 | 4 | 44 |
| **Sum** | 0 | 0 | $S_{xx} = 10$ | $S_{xy} = 104$ |

**(c)** $\hat\beta_1 = 104/10 = 10.4$ · $\;\hat\beta_0 = 50 - 10.4(2) = 29.2$

Each additional missed payment is associated with **10.4 percentage points
higher** utilization, on average.

::: {.notes}
Point at the two zeros in the Sum row for the deviation columns. Deviations
from the mean always sum to zero; she proved that in Classwork 2-1, 1(e).
Same fact, new place.

Keep this table on screen or on the board. You Try 3 builds on it.
:::

## Two facts OLS always guarantees

Fitted values: $\hat Y_i = 29.2 + 10.4 X_i$

| $i$ | $Y_i$ | $\hat Y_i$ | $\hat u_i = Y_i - \hat Y_i$ | $X_i \hat u_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30 | 29.2 | 0.8 | 0 |
| 2 | 38 | 39.6 | −1.6 | −1.6 |
| 3 | 52 | 50.0 | 2.0 | 4.0 |
| 4 | 58 | 60.4 | −2.4 | −7.2 |
| 5 | 72 | 70.8 | 1.2 | 4.8 |
| **Sum** | | | **0** | **0** |

. . .

1. **The residuals sum to zero:** $\sum \hat u_i = 0$. The line is not too
   high or too low on average.
2. **The residuals are uncorrelated with $X$:** $\sum X_i \hat u_i = 0$. The
   line has used up everything $X$ can linearly explain.

These are not luck. They are the two conditions that *define* the OLS line.
They are your arithmetic check on the homework.

::: {.notes}
If either sum is not zero (up to rounding) in her homework, there is an
arithmetic error upstream. Say that explicitly; it turns a theorem into a
debugging tool.

Fact 2, in plain words: if the residuals were still correlated with X, you
could tilt the line and do better. So at the best line, they are not.
:::

## Sums of squares: where the variation goes

The total variation in $Y$ splits exactly into two pieces:

$$
\underbrace{\sum (Y_i - \bar Y)^2}_{TSS} \;=\;
\underbrace{\sum (\hat Y_i - \bar Y)^2}_{ESS} \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum \hat u_i^{\,2}}_{SSR}
$$

| Stock & Watson | Name | What it measures | Where R puts it |
|---|---|---|---|
| $TSS$ | Total sum of squares | how much $Y$ varies around its mean | not printed; add the `Sum Sq` column |
| $ESS$ | Explained sum of squares | variation the **line** accounts for | `anova()`: the row named after $X$ |
| $SSR$ | Sum of squared residuals | variation the line **missed** | `anova()`: the `Residuals` row |

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §4.3. The textbook uses ESS / SSR / TSS. Your August notes
used SS_reg / SS_res / SS_tot. Same three objects. R's anova() table uses
neither name: it labels the explained row by the regressor's name.

The careful warning: SSR in Stock & Watson means the sum of squared
RESIDUALS. Some other books use SSR for the regression sum of squares. Tell
her to always check which convention a source is using. In this class SSR
is residuals.

Analogy that works: TSS is the whole pie. The line eats ESS. SSR is what is
left on the plate.
:::

## $R^2$ and the standard error of the regression

$$
R^2 \;=\; \frac{ESS}{TSS} \;=\; 1 - \frac{SSR}{TSS}
\qquad\qquad
SER \;=\; s_{\hat u} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{SSR}{n-2}}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**$R^2$**: the **share** of the variation in $Y$ explained by $X$. Between 0
and 1. No units.

$R^2$ is **not** a grade on the model. A low $R^2$ can still come with a
precisely estimated, important slope.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**SER**: the **typical size of a miss**, in the units of $Y$.

Divide by $n - 2$, not $n$: we used up two degrees of freedom estimating
$\hat\beta_0$ and $\hat\beta_1$.

R calls this the **Residual standard error**.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §4.3. Same n-1 logic as the sample variance on Day 3: each
estimated parameter costs one degree of freedom. With one regressor we
estimated two parameters, so n-2.

Common misreading to kill: "R-squared of 0.24 means the model is bad." In
the portfolio, FICO explains about a quarter of the variation in utilization.
For one variable that is substantial. Credit risk models routinely run with
modest R-squared and are still useful.
:::

## You Try 3 — Finish the five accounts

Use the residuals from two slides ago and your table from You Try 2.

**(a)** Compute $TSS = \sum (Y_i - \bar Y)^2$.

**(b)** Compute $SSR = \sum \hat u_i^{\,2}$.

**(c)** Compute $ESS$ two ways: as $TSS - SSR$, and directly as
$\hat\beta_1^{\,2}\, S_{xx}$. Do they agree?

**(d)** Compute $R^2$ and the $SER$. Interpret each in one sentence.

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes.

(c) uses a shortcut she has not seen: with one regressor, ESS = beta1-hat
squared times S_xx. Why: Y-hat minus Y-bar = beta1-hat (X - X-bar), square
it and sum. Show it on the board after she has computed both numbers and seen
that they agree. The shortcut saves a lot of arithmetic on the homework.
:::

## Solution 3

**(a)** $TSS = (-20)^2 + (-12)^2 + 2^2 + 8^2 + 22^2 = 400 + 144 + 4 + 64 + 484 = 1096$

**(b)** $SSR = 0.8^2 + 1.6^2 + 2.0^2 + 2.4^2 + 1.2^2 = 0.64 + 2.56 + 4 + 5.76 + 1.44 = 14.4$

**(c)** $ESS = 1096 - 14.4 = 1081.6$ · and $\;\hat\beta_1^2 S_{xx} = 10.4^2 \times 10 = 108.16 \times 10 = 1081.6$ ✓

**(d)** $R^2 = 1081.6 / 1096 = 0.9869$: missed payments explain about 98.7%
of the variation in utilization across these five accounts.

$SER = \sqrt{14.4 / (5 - 2)} = \sqrt{4.8} = 2.19$: the line typically misses
by about 2.2 percentage points.

::: {.notes}
An R-squared of 0.99 is a warning, not a triumph. Five hand-picked accounts
almost on a line is not what real data look like. The 500-account portfolio
gives about 0.24, and that is the realistic number.

Bridge to the break: "Everything you just did by hand, R does in one line.
After the break we make R show its work."
:::

## How sure are we about $\hat\beta_1$?

A different 500 accounts would give a **different** $\hat\beta_1$. Like
$\bar Y$ on Day 4, $\hat\beta_1$ is a **random variable** with a sampling
distribution (S&W §4.5).

. . .

Its standard deviation is estimated by the **standard error**:

$$
SE(\hat\beta_1) \;=\; \frac{SER}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
\;=\; \sqrt{\frac{SSR/(n-2)}{\sum (X_i - \bar X)^2}}
$$

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**SE shrinks when:**

- the line misses less (small SER)
- $X$ is spread out (big $S_{xx}$)
- you have more data ($S_{xx}$ grows with $n$)
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
Five accounts: $SE = 2.19/\sqrt{10} = 0.693$.

So $\hat\beta_1 = 10.4$ with a standard error of about 0.7. **Tuesday** we
ask whether 10.4 is far from zero *in units of that 0.7*.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the formula R's summary() uses: the homoskedasticity-only standard
error (Stock & Watson §5.4). The textbook prefers robust standard errors,
which allow the spread of u to vary with X. At this level, use R's default
and know that the alternative exists. Tuesday has a one-line mention.

Intuition for "X spread out": if every account had nearly the same FICO,
you could not learn the slope at all. Leverage comes from variation in X.
Draw two scatters on the board, one with X bunched, one with X spread.
:::

# Hour 2 · Code

## The portfolio, simulated

```{r}
#| label: sim-show
#| eval: false
set.seed(1105)
n <- 500
fico <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 690, 50), 560), 830)) # scores between 560 and 830
util <- 160 - 0.15 * fico + rnorm(n, 0, 12) # the TRUE line, plus noise
util <- round(pmin(pmax(util, 0), 100), 1) # utilization stays in 0-100
cards <- tibble(fico, util)
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-peek
head(cards, 4)
```

We **wrote down the truth**: $\beta_0 = 160$, $\beta_1 = -0.15$. Real data
never tells you that. Simulated data does, so we can check whether OLS finds
it.

::: {.notes}
This is the advantage of simulation she saw on Day 4: we know the answer, so
we can grade the estimator.

pmin and pmax just clip values into a range. Do not spend time on them.
:::

## You Try 4 — OLS by hand, in R

Complete the code. Then check it against `lm()`.

```{r}
#| label: you-try-4
#| eval: false
x <- cards$fico
y <- cards$util

Sxx <- sum((x - mean(x))^____)
Sxy <- sum((x - ____) * (y - ____))

b1 <- ____ / ____
b0 <- mean(y) - ____ * mean(x)
c(b0 = b0, b1 = b1)

reg <- lm(util ~ fico, data = cards)
coef(reg) # do they match?
```

How close is $\hat\beta_1$ to the true $-0.15$? Should it be exact?

::: {.notes}
Six minutes. These are the exact steps of You Try 2, typed instead of
written. Make that link out loud.

The "should it be exact" question is Day 4 again: no, the estimate has
sampling error. It will be close, not equal.
:::

## Solution 4

```{r}
#| label: you-try-4-soln
x <- cards$fico
y <- cards$util

Sxx <- sum((x - mean(x))^2)
Sxy <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y)))

b1 <- Sxy / Sxx
b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x)
c(b0 = b0, b1 = b1)
coef(lm(util ~ fico, data = cards))
```

They match to every digit. And $\hat\beta_1 \approx$ `r round(coef(reg)[2], 3)`
is close to the truth, $-0.15$, but not equal: that gap is **sampling error**.

::: {.notes}
Pause on the match. `lm()` is not magic; it computes the formula she just
wrote. Everything in the regression table is arithmetic she can do.
:::

## You Try 5 — Sums of squares in R

```{r}
#| label: you-try-5
#| eval: false
yhat <- fitted(reg) # the line's predictions
uhat <- resid(reg) # the misses

c(sum_u = sum(uhat), sum_xu = sum(x * uhat)) # the two OLS facts

TSS <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
ESS <- sum((____ - mean(y))^2)
SSR <- sum(____^2)
c(TSS = TSS, ESS_plus_SSR = ESS + SSR) # should be equal

R2 <- ____ / ____
SER <- sqrt(____ / (length(y) - ____))
c(R2 = R2, SER = SER)

summary(reg) # find R2 and SER in the output
anova(reg) # find ESS and SSR in the output
```

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes. Then put summary(reg) and anova(reg) on screen side by side
and have her POINT to each number she computed. Pointing is the skill. The
homework asks her to fill in these exact two printouts.

sum_u and sum_xu will print as numbers like 1e-12. That is zero, up to
floating-point rounding. Worth thirty seconds: computers store decimals
imperfectly.
:::

## Solution 5

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r}
#| label: you-try-5-soln
yhat <- fitted(reg)
uhat <- resid(reg)
TSS <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
ESS <- sum((yhat - mean(y))^2)
SSR <- sum(uhat^2)
R2 <- ESS / TSS
SER <- sqrt(SSR / (length(y) - 2))
round(c(TSS = TSS, ESS = ESS, SSR = SSR, R2 = R2, SER = SER), 3)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{r}
#| label: anova-5
anova(reg)
```

- `fico` row, `Sum Sq` = **ESS**
- `Residuals` row, `Sum Sq` = **SSR**
- $TSS$ = the two added together
- `Residuals` `Mean Sq` $= SSR/(n-2) = SER^2$
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The Mean Sq for Residuals is SER squared. Have her take the square root of
it and find the "Residual standard error" line in summary(). Same number.

Leave the F value column alone today. It is Tuesday's material; say "we'll
come back for that column."
:::

## You Try 6 — Make the slope bounce

The Std. Error claims to measure how much $\hat\beta_1$ moves from sample to
sample. **Test that claim.** Draw 1,000 new portfolios from the same truth,
and re-estimate the slope each time.

```{r}
#| label: you-try-6
#| eval: false
set.seed(300)
slopes <- replicate(1000, {
  fico <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(500, 690, 50), 560), 830))
  util <- pmin(pmax(160 - 0.15 * fico + rnorm(500, 0, 12), 0), 100)
  coef(lm(util ~ fico))[____] # which element is the slope?
})

c(mean_of_slopes = mean(____), sd_of_slopes = sd(____))
coef(summary(reg))["fico", "Std. Error"] # what ONE sample estimated
hist(slopes, breaks = 40)
```

**(a)** Is the average slope close to $-0.15$? **(b)** Is the SD of the
slopes close to the Std. Error from our one sample?

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes. This is the payoff of the day, and it is Day 4's You Try 3
with a slope in place of a mean.

(a) yes: OLS is unbiased under the assumptions (S&W §4.4-4.5). (b) yes:
the SE, computed from ONE sample, predicts the spread across a thousand
samples we never see. That is what a standard error is for.

The histogram will be bell-shaped. Ask why. Answer: the CLT, applied to
the slope.
:::

## Solution 6

```{r}
#| label: you-try-6-soln
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(300)
slopes <- replicate(1000, {
  fico <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(500, 690, 50), 560), 830))
  util <- pmin(pmax(160 - 0.15 * fico + rnorm(500, 0, 12), 0), 100)
  coef(lm(util ~ fico))[2]
})
round(
  c(
    mean = mean(slopes),
    sd = sd(slopes),
    one_sample_SE = coef(summary(reg))["fico", "Std. Error"]
  ),
  4
)
ggplot(tibble(slopes), aes(slopes)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.15, linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

::: {.notes}
Two numbers to point at: the SD of 1,000 slopes and the SE from one sample.
They agree to about two decimal places. Say: "When you read Std. Error in a
table, you are reading this histogram's width, estimated from one dataset."

Bell shape plus a known width is all Tuesday's t-test needs.
:::

## The top half of a regression table

```{r}
#| label: coef-table
coef(summary(reg))
```

| Column | Symbol | Formula | Today? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Estimate | $\hat\beta_j$ | $S_{xy}/S_{xx}$; $\;\bar Y - \hat\beta_1 \bar X$ | ✓ |
| Std. Error | $SE(\hat\beta_j)$ | $SER/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$ for the slope | ✓ |
| t value | $t$ | $\hat\beta_j / SE(\hat\beta_j)$ | **Tuesday** |
| Pr(>\|t\|) | $p$ | area in the $t$ tails | **Tuesday** |

::: {.notes}
Ask her to read the fico row out loud as a sentence: "Each extra FICO point
is associated with about 0.14 points lower utilization, and that estimate
would typically move by about 0.011 from sample to sample."

Then ask: 0.14 is about thirteen of those 0.011s away from zero. Is that a
lot? Let her answer, and tell her Tuesday makes that question precise.
:::

## Day 5 on one page

| Idea | What it says | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| Linear model | outcome = line + error | $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + u_i$ |
| OLS | the line with the smallest squared misses | $\min \sum \hat u_i^2$ |
| Slope | covariance over variance | $\hat\beta_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ |
| Intercept | line passes through the means | $\hat\beta_0 = \bar Y - \hat\beta_1 \bar X$ |
| OLS facts | residuals sum to 0, uncorrelated with $X$ | $\sum \hat u_i = 0,\ \sum X_i \hat u_i = 0$ |
| Sums of squares | variation splits exactly | $TSS = ESS + SSR$ |
| $R^2$ | share explained | $ESS/TSS$ |
| SER | typical miss, in $Y$ units | $\sqrt{SSR/(n-2)}$ |
| $SE(\hat\beta_1)$ | how much the slope bounces | $SER/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$ |

# Appendix: the same thing in Python {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.notes}
NOT part of the count. Do not present. Assign as reading, or use if the code

:::

## OLS and sums of squares in Python {visibility="uncounted"}

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(1105)
fico = np.clip(np.round(rng.normal(690, 50, 500)), 560, 830)
util = np.clip(160 - 0.15 * fico + rng.normal(0, 12, 500), 0, 100).round(1)
cards = pd.DataFrame({"fico": fico, "util": util})

# by hand
x, y = cards.fico, cards.util
b1 = ((x - x.mean()) * (y - y.mean())).sum() / ((x - x.mean())**2).sum()
b0 = y.mean() - b1 * x.mean()

# by statsmodels (the R lm() equivalent)
reg = smf.ols("util ~ fico", data=cards).fit()
reg.params            # b0, b1
reg.ess, reg.ssr      # ESS and SSR -- statsmodels uses the S&W names
reg.rsquared          # R^2
np.sqrt(reg.mse_resid)  # SER
reg.bse               # standard errors
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
Python's random numbers differ from R's even with the same seed, so the
estimates will be close to the R ones but not identical.
:::
